prompt :
Create an ultra-realistic premium editorial portrait using the PROVIDED PERSON REFERENCE IMAGE as the STRICT IDENTITY REFERENCE.

The supplied reference image controls the identity, facial appearance, hairstyle, hair texture, skin tone, facial proportions, body proportions, and recognizable characteristics of the MAIN PERSON.

IMPORTANT:

Preserve the exact recognizable identity of the supplied person.

Do not replace the face with a generic model.

Do not redesign the person's facial features.

Do not change the person's age, skin tone, face shape, eye shape, nose, lips, eyebrows, or distinctive characteristics.

Create ONE SINGLE VERTICAL COMPOSITE IMAGE divided into TWO HALVES by a dramatic irregular vertical torn-paper transition.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

LEFT HALF — REAL PHOTOGRAPH

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

On the LEFT side, show the supplied person as a completely photorealistic, high-end fashion portrait.

The person should look exactly like the supplied reference identity.

Pose:

- confident relaxed standing pose

- upper-body / three-quarter portrait

- face turned slightly toward the camera

- calm, confident editorial expression

- natural posture

- realistic human anatomy

Wardrobe:

Create a sophisticated modern fashion outfit inspired by the target image:

a fitted black top underneath an elegant warm rust / burnt-orange blazer or jacket.

Preserve realistic fabric texture, stitching, folds, shadows and natural clothing behavior.

HAIR:

Maintain the person's reference hairstyle and hair characteristics as accurately as possible.

Individual hair strands must be visible.

Natural volume and realistic movement.

LIGHTING:

Soft natural daylight.

Subtle cinematic highlights.

Realistic facial shadows.

Natural skin texture.

Professional fashion photography lighting.

BACKGROUND:

Modern contemporary architectural environment with a large glass-and-steel building facade.

Tall vertical windows and structural lines behind the subject.

Soft realistic depth of field.

Clean urban editorial atmosphere.

The LEFT HALF must look like a genuine professional photograph.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

RIGHT HALF — HAND-DRAWN COMIC VERSION

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

On the RIGHT side, recreate the SAME PERSON as a sophisticated monochrome hand-drawn fashion illustration.

The illustrated person must clearly resemble the exact person from the supplied reference image.

Preserve:

- same face identity

- same hairstyle

- same facial proportions

- same approximate pose

- same body proportions

- same clothing silhouette

Transform ONLY the visual medium into a detailed black-and-white editorial comic illustration.

Illustration style:

- hand-drawn ink artwork

- sophisticated fashion illustration

- clean black outlines

- subtle grayscale shading

- realistic anatomy

- elegant sketchbook quality

- expressive facial details

- carefully drawn hair strands

- professional graphic-novel / fashion-comic aesthetic

Do NOT make it childish.

Do NOT make it cartoonish.

Do NOT use anime style.

Do NOT use exaggerated comic proportions.

The illustrated person should feel like a high-fashion black-and-white graphic novel character based directly on the real person.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

CENTER TRANSITION — TORN PAPER

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Create a dramatic irregular VERTICAL TORN-PAPER DIVISION between the real photograph and the illustration.

The split should NOT be a clean straight line.

It must look like REAL PAPER being torn vertically from the top to the bottom.

Create:

- irregular jagged edges

- uneven ripped-paper fibers

- realistic paper thickness

- subtle white paper fibers

- tiny torn fragments

- slight shadow along the ripped edge

- natural imperfect tearing

- convincing physical paper texture

The torn edge should reveal a clear transition from:

PHOTOREALISTIC PERSON → HAND-DRAWN ILLUSTRATION.

The transition must feel physically layered and believable.

Do not use a simple digital split-screen effect.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

ILLUSTRATION DETAILS

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Add tasteful hand-drawn doodle elements around the illustrated half, similar to a creative fashion sketchbook:

small cloud

small stars

small heart

simple coffee cup

small vintage camera

tiny decorative sparkles

These elements must be black-and-white hand-drawn ink doodles.

Keep them subtle and aesthetically balanced.

Do not overcrowd the image.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

MATCHING BETWEEN BOTH HALVES

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

The REAL and ILLUSTRATED versions must represent the SAME PERSON.

Their:

- face

- hairstyle

- pose

- clothing

- body proportions

- overall silhouette

must visually correspond across the torn-paper boundary.

The left side is REAL.

The right side is the HAND-DRAWN artistic interpretation of that same person.

Make the transition look intentional and seamless.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

VISUAL STYLE

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Luxury fashion editorial.

Creative advertising campaign.

Premium magazine photography.

Photorealistic + hand-drawn mixed-media artwork.

Modern artistic portrait.

Sophisticated minimal composition.

High-end visual storytelling.

The final image should look like a professionally designed fashion campaign rather than an ordinary AI-generated image.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

CAMERA

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Eye-level camera.

Straight-on perspective.

Medium / three-quarter portrait.

Natural lens perspective.

No fisheye distortion.

No extreme wide-angle distortion.

Sharp focus on the main subject.

Realistic depth of field.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

COLOR

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

LEFT SIDE:

Natural full color.

Warm realistic skin tones.

Burnt-orange / rust clothing.

Neutral architectural background.

RIGHT SIDE:

Strict black-and-white / grayscale.

White paper background.

Black ink outlines.

Soft gray shading.

Keep the two visual worlds clearly distinguishable.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

OUTPUT QUALITY

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Ultra-photorealistic.

Extremely detailed.

Professional editorial quality.

Natural skin pores.

Realistic hair strands.

Detailed clothing texture.

Highly detailed ink illustration.

Fine paper fibers.

Accurate anatomy.

Clean composition.

Premium commercial advertising quality.

TARGET OUTPUT RESOLUTION:

16K ULTRA HIGH RESOLUTION

15360 × 8640 pixels

approximately 132.7 million pixels.

If the image-generation system cannot natively generate 15360 × 8640 pixels, generate at the highest available resolution while preserving maximum detail, composition, identity consistency, and fine texture, optimized for high-quality 16K upscaling.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

STRICT NEGATIVE PROMPT

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

different person, changed identity, generic face, face replacement, face swap, identity drift, altered facial structure, different hairstyle, different hair color, different skin tone, different age, inconsistent face, two different people, duplicate person, extra person, extra limbs, extra fingers, deformed hands, bad anatomy, distorted body, unrealistic proportions, plastic skin, wax skin, CGI, 3D render, anime, childish cartoon, low-quality cartoon, colorful illustration, straight split line, clean digital divider, smooth transition, messy torn paper, fake paper edge, excessive doodles, cluttered background, distorted architecture, blurry face, low resolution, oversharpening, excessive HDR, artificial skin, unrealistic clothing, random text, typography, logo, watermark, signature, captions.

Generative Art was here befoe AI: 
Before computers. The idea starts as instruction plus chance.Mozart-era musical dice games let rules assemble minuets. Dada and Cage used chance operations so the artist would not control every event. Sol LeWitt’s wall drawings made the score the work: written rules, executed by other hands. Constructivism and Op art trained people to think in systems, grids, and variation. Jacquard looms and Ada Lovelace’s 1843 notes on Babbage already implied that a machine following a procedure could do more than calculate — it could compose. 

https://t.co/dzNa0FkX6w

That is the prehistory: the artist writes conditions; something else completes the picture.1960s: plotters and the AlgoristsThe first public computer-art shows happen in 1965.Georg Nees exhibits plotter drawings in Stuttgart in February 1965. Frieder Nake follows. In New York, A. Michael Noll and Béla Julesz show computer-generated pictures at Howard Wise Gallery. Noll had started deliberately making “computer art” at Bell Labs in 1962 after a plotter bug produced a mess someone joked was art. He then programmed order plus disorder on purpose. 

https://t.co/Uwx4OQ3ZpJ

Nees’s Schotter (Gravel) is the textbook image of that idea: a grid of squares that begins regular and tilts into chaos as it descends. The work is not “the computer drew a picture.” It is a rule about how much disorder to https://t.co/0AC8vq4Qc8

Vera Molnár is the other pillar. In Paris she invented a machine imaginaire — executing algorithms by hand — before she got mainframe access in 1968. Then FORTRAN, BASIC, plotters. Grids, letters, controlled percentages of disorder. She came from painting and Constructivism, not from a lab demo. 

https://t.co/XYpbjyWDpz

https://t.co/v1g9yyoV32

Around them: Manfred Mohr, Charles Csuri (Sine Curve Man, 1967), Hiroshi Kawano, Herbert Franke, Lillian Schwartz, John and James Whitney in film. Jean-Pierre Hébert later named this loose family the Algorists: artists who write algorithms as their medium. 

https://t.co/GZAtxx872N

1968: the public discovers the fieldJasia Reichardt’s Cybernetic Serendipity at London’s ICA (2 August–20 October 1968) is the first big international survey of computers and the arts. Graphics, films, generated music, robots, cybernetic sculptures. Artists, engineers, and composers in one room. Tens of thousands of visitors. It tours to Washington and San Francisco. Harold Cohen later said seeing that show helped push him toward machine art. 

https://t.co/pssQ14IIuz

MoMA’s The Machine as Seen at the End of the Mechanical Age (also 1968) and later Software at the Jewish Museum (1970) keep the argument inside institutions: is the program the work, or the print it leaves behind? 

https://t.co/XYpbjyWDpz

Cohen and AARON: the long AI projectHarold Cohen, already a painter who had represented Britain at Venice, starts AARON in the early 1970s after time at Stanford’s AI Lab. It is not a prompt box. It is a drawing program he rewrites for decades: first abstract marks, then plants and figures, then color. AARON draws; Cohen designs what AARON is allowed to know about composition, closure, and form. Museums let it work in public at SFMOMA and the Tate. That is still the cleanest historical example of an artist building a collaborator instead of renting a generator. 

https://t.co/t30TGbBoaF

https://t.co/ADGTFNhWV6

https://t.co/FoDccQZBNP

1980s–1990s: fractals, scenes, closed shopsMandelbrot’s fractals leak into popular “computer art.” Plotter and algorithmic artists keep working with less fashion heat. The demoscene treats realtime code as craft. John Maeda’s Design By Numbers at MIT tries to give visual people a programming language small enough to sketch with. Flash becomes a mass tool for motion systems. The through-line is the same: code as pencil, not code as vending machine.2001: ProcessingCasey Reas and Ben Fry release Processing, built out of Maeda’s MIT orbit. Goal: artists and designers write systems the way they used to sketch. Reas’s own Process series is explicit LeWitt-into-software: rules for elements and behaviors, then the program runs. Jared Tarbell, Marius Watz, and a generation of “creative coders” come out of that stack. Open source matters here. The tool is inspectable. The system can be shown, not only the JPEG. 

https://t.co/ADGTFNhWV6

2014–2018: GANs become “the look”Ian Goodfellow’s generative adversarial networks (2014) give artists a new engine: a generator tries to fool a discriminator trained on a dataset. Mario Klingemann, Helena Sarin, and others treat the network as a material you tune — datasets, thresholds, failure modes. Refik Anadol scales data-trained “hallucinations” into museums. 

https://t.co/KdiRsEww0Z

The market event is Obvious’s Portrait of Edmond de Belamy at Christie’s in 2018: $432,500. A blurry invented aristocrat, signed with a GAN formula. It made “AI art” a headline and also a fight. Many working GAN artists pointed out that Obvious used an existing model and training approach; the auction sold the idea of machine authorship more than a deep studio practice. That split — spectacle versus built system — never went away. 

https://t.co/M9cFVWkrci

Prompt :
Use each uploaded image as the only visual source.Create one independent poster per upload and output each separately.Never combine images.Role:You are an art director skilled in vintage offset print,comic halftones,pop posters,and magazine-style visual distillation. Design a vertical 3:4 print-quality diptych poster with an editorial collectible feel.Format:Split the canvas into two strictly equal horizontal panels,top 50% and bottom 50%,with an exact 1:1 division.Upper panel:Present the uploaded reference image in the top half.Keep the original subject,scene identity,main objects,gesture,spatial relationships,and emotional atmosphere recognizable.Preserve it as image-based rather than https://t.co/yd6fQLU2cV may crop naturally to fit the panel,but never stretch,distort,mirror,replace,or redesign the subject.Apply only restrained editorial grading and subtle print refinement.Lower panel:Transform the same source into a retro offset-halftone pop poster.Extract the strongest action,the clearest object silhouettes,the main emotional tension,and the essential color relationships from the upper image.Rebuild them with bold black outlines,large flat color fields,visible halftone dots,slight registration misalignment,minor ink spread,small printing imperfections,and controlled burst-like negative space.The lower half should be more distilled and graphic than the upper half,yet still instantly recognizable as the same scene or https://t.co/dv3ALeMvDu:Blend vintage offset lithography,pop-graphic poster design,magazine cover composition,indie publication aesthetics,and restrained comic-print language.The result should feel sophisticated and collectible,not loud or cheap.Use only 4 to 5 main colors.The lower half may be brighter than the upper half,but keep the palette controlled.Preserve paper grain,subtle ink shift,light fold traces,and retro print noise.Avoid glossy smoothness.Composition:Give the lower half a magazine-cover hierarchy with one dominant focal idea and supporting shapes.Use strong silhouette simplification,clear rhythm,and strategic blank areas.Suggest energy through scale contrast and white space,but do not fill the frame with clutter.Typography:You may add a small amount of English-only text in the lower half,such as a short title,onomatopoeia,a tiny cover line,or a small price-tag detail,but only when it supports the composition.Text must stay legible,sparse,and secondary.Overall feeling:An independent-publication cover,art-exhibition poster,or collectible visual-research page.Calm,modern,restrained,and premium.The top half presents the source;the bottom half turns that source into a refined retro halftone pop interpretation.Negative:No childish cartoon,no cheap sticker look,no sales-promo poster,no garbled text,no pseudo text,no uncontrolled colors,no full-screen blast elements,no 3D rendering,no realistic copying in the lower half,no overly cute styling,no oversized subject,no watermark,no logo,no UI.

These 15 AI tools can help you👇

Chat and Research
1. ChatGPT : A versatile conversational AI for writing, brainstorming, and coding.

2. Claude: An advanced AI assistant by Anthropic known for deep analysis and long-form writing.

3. Google Gemini: Google's multi-modal AI integrated across search and workspace apps.

4. Perplexity: An AI-powered search engine that provides direct answers with source citations.

Image and Design
5. Midjourney: A top-tier text-to-image generator for hyper-realistic and artistic visuals.

6. Canva AI: An easy design platform with built-in AI tools for social media and presentations.

7. Ideogram: An AI image creator specializing in clear typography and graphic text placement.

Video and Audio
8. Runway: A creative suite for AI video generation, editing, and cinematic effects.

9. ElevenLabs: A realistic voice generator with lifelike text-to-speech and voice cloning.

10. Descript: An audio and video editor that lets you edit media by modifying text transcripts.

Coding and Development
11. Cursor: An AI-first code editor designed to help developers write and debug code faster.

12. Lovable: A "vibe-coding" tool that lets non-technical users build software apps using simple descriptions.

Productivity and Automation
13. Zapier Central: An AI automation platform that connects different apps to perform tasks for you.

14. Notion AI: A workspace assistant that summarizes notes, writes content, and organizes data.

15. Gamma: An AI tool that instantly builds polished presentations, memos, and web pages from text prompts.

The main reason people are getting rejected for X's Monetisation, is spam and unoriginal content. If you look at it, once a news breaks, every account is sharing the same image, with the same content just reworded in their own style. For the algorithm, it might seem repetitive content. 

They really want something that is unique and more personal to creators. Maybe something exclusive, like an original finding, research, opinion, on-ground reporting or podcast bytes. It can be in the form of text, image or videos. Not just clipping and reposting other's news and stuff.
